For example, the only population of the Devil's Hole pupfish, a species endemic to the desert of Ash Meadows, Nevada, is found in a bedroom-sized spring welling up in the desert. Its habitat is threatened by development of the desert with irrigation requiring excessive withdrawals of water from the underground aquifer which also supplies Devil's Hole spring. The species apparently evolved in the spring where it now lives. The population, which varies from 300 to 800, depending upon the time of the annual cycle, is probably as large as it ever has been, and protection of the population and habitat will result in no change in the immediate environment except stabilization of ground water levels.
The Okaloosa darter is and always has been confined to five small streams which originate on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and empty into the Gulf nearby. The population, which is said to be less than 1,500 fish, is threatened by deteriorating habitat and probable competition from other darters. Restoration of the species would mean development of healthier populations in the same streams in which they are now located.
Within the past 25 to 40 years the Great Lakes have undergone drastic evolution stimulated by development of the St. Lawrence Seaway and increasing volumes of pollution. The result has been the immigration of intensive predators and competitors, including the lamprey and alewife, from the ocean, and rapidly increasing eutrophication of the once limitless waters. Many of the fishes so abundant in the lakes only a few years ago have been sadly depleted and some are on the verge of extirpation, if they are not already extinct. Among these are the longjaw cisco which may survive in the deeper parts of Lakes Michigan and Huron and the blue pike, once a prized food fish in Lake Erie.
